entry.title: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours

link.title: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours

entry.content:
A while back, I shared [a sneak peek at a project I was working on](https://peakd.com/hive-139531/@asgarth/a-sneak-peek-at-a-new-project-coming-soon). There were screenshots, quite a few themes, and a conveniently vague “coming soon.” Well, it finally has a link I can share. PeakD Blog is live at **[peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog).** The idea is simple: give your Hive writing a home that feels like your own website. Your posts, your profile, your style, and an address you can put on a business card, share with a friend, or add to your social profiles. ## Your writing, with a place of its own If you already publish on PeakD, you already have the content to get started. ![image.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/asgarth/23u6Yr2NYjaoznaioWdQMDMBKEid8Z1114ivw9qsS4q2zVpXKsEb2wJjnqX328ziuL6T4.png) PeakD Blog brings your existing Hive posts together in a dedicated blog, with an archive, individual article pages, and About and Contact pages based on your Hive profile. You keep publishing through PeakD, and your posts appear on your blog. The content stays on Hive, and your blog settings are saved in your account metadata. Once you've claimed your blog, anyone can open it and read your articles without signing in or having a Hive account. That makes it an easy link to share with people who are interested in your writing and might be discovering Hive for the first time. PeakD remains the place to write, discover communities, and take part in the wider Hive experience. Your blog gives people a place to spend time with your work. ## Pick a look that feels like you If you read the preview, you might remember that I got a little carried away with the themes. That hasn't really changed. There are clean personal blogs, photography-focused designs, bold typography, field notebooks, retro pixels, and terminal-inspired layouts. The themes have their own character, including how they handle navigation, archives, and article pages. **Default, Minimalist, Brutalist, and Aperture are available to everyone**, with more designs choices available through [PeakD Horizon](https://peakd.com/@peakd/subscriptions). Depending on the theme, you can choose top or side navigation, list or grid views, content width, light or dark mode, and accent colors. You can also change your blog's name and description, preview your choices, and save them through your wallet. I wanted this part to be fun: try a few things, find something you like, and get back to writing. ## A few useful details Alongside the design choices, there are some practical features to help people enjoy and follow your work: - **Topic browsing:** enable a topic bar so readers can find more posts about the subjects they like. - **RSS:** readers can follow your blog in their preferred feed reader. - **Sharing:** article pages include sharing options and previews for links shared elsewhere. - **Mobile layouts:** your blog adapts to phones, tablets, and larger screens. - **Interface languages:** optional localization lets readers use the navigation and interface in their preferred supported language. Your articles stay in the language you wrote them in. And the Hive connection is still there. Readers with a Hive account can connect a supported wallet, choose their vote weight, comment, and reply directly on the blog. Those interactions happen on Hive, with signing handled by the wallet. ## A little more room with Horizon You can get started for free. The free blog shows posts published through PeakD and includes the four free themes mentioned above. An active **[PeakD Horizon subscription](https://peakd.com/@peakd/subscriptions) for the blog owner** adds: - **Posts from other Hive publishing apps**, so your blog can bring together writing published across Hive. - **Premium themes**, for more ways to make the site your own. - **Up to three posts pinned in your navigation**, useful for a “Start here” guide, a project introduction, or information you want visitors to find easily. - **A portfolio gallery**, displaying images from posts you've marked “Show in Portfolio” on PeakD, with topic filters and a full-screen image viewer. If you already have Horizon on the account that owns your blog, those extras are available to that blog. Readers don't need Horizon to visit it. ## More than a place for the latest post This is the part I'm looking forward to seeing people use. A travel writer could turn years of posts into a journal worth exploring. A photographer or artist could pair their stories with a portfolio. Someone building a project could pin an introduction and keep publishing updates under one address. There is also a **Products page for accounts with their Hive shop enabled**, bringing existing product and subscription listings into the blog. That gives people another way to discover what you offer alongside your writing. You may already have a lot of useful work on Hive. A dedicated blog gives you another way to put it in front of people, including people outside our usual circles. ## Give it a try Getting started is straightforward: 1. Visit **[peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog)** and enter your Hive username. 2. Connect the wallet for that account to open your owner preview. 3. Open **Customize blog**, try the available settings, and preview the result. 4. Choose **Claim & Save** and approve the operation in your wallet. 5. Share **`yourname.peakd.blog`** and keep publishing through PeakD. Until you claim it, the blog preview is only accessible to you as the owner. Claiming makes the blog public; your existing Hive posts remain public on Hive throughout. If you're new to Hive, you can [create an account](https://signup.hive.io/) first and start from there. I'm happy to finally get this into people's hands. If you set up a blog, drop your link in the comments — I'd love to see which themes you choose and what you do with it. Feedback, suggestions, and the inevitable “this looks a bit strange on my phone” reports are welcome here or [on Discord](https://discord.gg/uPxmXjX). **[Come have a look at peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog).**
Source: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours by @asgarth

entry.title: HafSQL v2.7.0
entry.content:
# HafSQL v2.7.0: changes for public database users ## Removed tables - **`hafsql.rc_delegations_table`** is gone. Use the `hafsql.rc_delegations` view, which now reads from balance_tracker. - **`hafsql.proposal_approvals_table`** is gone. Use the `hafsql.proposal_approvals` view, which now reads from hafbe. ## Removed columns from `hafsql.accounts_table` `reward_hive_balance`, `reward_hbd_balance`, `reward_vests_balance`, `to_withdraw`, `vesting_withdraw_rate`, `withdrawn` and `proxy` are gone. The `hafsql.accounts` **view** still has all of them under the same names. They now come from balance_tracker / hafbe. If you queried `accounts_table` directly, switch to the view. ## View columns that changed (same names, different values or types) | View.column | Before | Now | |---|---|---| | `delegations.vests` | raw ×1,000,000 | VESTS, `numeric(27,6)` | | `accounts.incoming_vests` / `outgoing_vests` | raw ×1,000,000 | VESTS. `*_hp` columns unchanged | | `accounts.to_withdraw` | remaining amount, dropped after each payout | total power-down amount (as in hived) | | `accounts.vesting_withdraw_rate` | to_withdraw / 13 | rounded up, as hived does since HF21 | | `accounts.next_vesting_withdrawal` | drifted 3s per weekly payout | exact. `NULL` when no power down is active | | `rc_delegations.rc` | `text` | numeric | | `rc_delegations.timestamp` | last sync time of the row | block time of the delegation op | | `comments.net_rshares` | sum of absolute rshares | signed sum (downvotes subtract) | | `comments.abs_rshares` | n/a | **new column**: sum of absolute rshares | | `comments.total_rshares` / `net_rshares` | changed votes counted twice | only each voter's latest vote counts | | `operation_account_update*_table.json_metadata` / `posting_json_metadata` | `{}` when the op left it empty | `NULL` (empty means "unchanged" on chain) | ## Behavior changes - **Comments deleted and then re-posted** at the same permlink are now a new row with a **new `id`**, the same as hivemind. Before, they stayed marked as deleted. - **Weekly market buckets** now run Monday to Sunday. Before, Sunday trades landed in the next week. Existing buckets are rebuilt. - **`hafsql.get_timestamp`, `hafsql.id_from_timestamp` and `comments.cashout_time` / `last_payout`** now give correct results when your session timezone isn't UTC. - **`hafsql.get_timestamp`** now also accepts a block number (`int4`). - **`hafd.operation_id_to_type_id`** was removed from the docs. ## Fixes (no query changes needed) - Reblog permlinks were wrong. - Account metadata was wiped by updates with empty metadata. - Comment titles were blanked by edits with an empty title. - `get_balance(account, block)` and `balances_history` were slow.
Source: HafSQL v2.7.0 by @mahdiyari

entry.title: PR #141: Letting Hive-Engine Lite Nodes Catch Up Before Cleaning House

link.title: PR #141: Letting Hive-Engine Lite Nodes Catch Up Before Cleaning House

entry.content:
Hey everyone, In my last update, I broke down the Knobs A, B, and C changes and teased what was coming next. The latest piece of that puzzle, **Knobs D**, is now built, tested on live mainnet traffic, and submitted as [PR #141](https://github.com/hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts/pull/141) against the `qa` branch. This round focuses squarely on lite-node operations: specifically, teaching the node to hold off on pruning local database history when it has more urgent work to do. ## The Problem: Housekeeping During a Fire Lite nodes stay small and efficient by periodically running cleanup jobs (`database.cleanupLightNode()`) to purge old blocks and transactions they no longer need. Under normal conditions, this background housekeeping runs quietly and everyone is happy. The trouble starts when a node falls behind. Whether it's scheduled server maintenance, an unexpected reboot, or an upstream network hiccup, a node that wakes up thousands of blocks behind the chain head needs all the CPU cycles and disk I/O it can get just to ingest and validate incoming blocks. Having MongoDB stop what it's doing every few minutes to execute heavy delete operations right in the middle of a catch-up sprint is the database equivalent of vacuuming the living room while the house is on fire. It causes unnecessary I/O contention and drags out the time it takes to get back to the head block. The fix is straightforward in concept: make cleanup lag-aware. If the node is struggling to catch up, let it defer cleanup for a bit and focus on block ingestion. Crucially, this doesn't touch block processing order, smart contracts, or consensus rules. It strictly changes _when_ local pruning takes place. ## The New Configuration Knobs The adaptive cleanup behavior is completely opt-in and controlled under the `lightNode` configuration block: ```json { "lightNode": { "enabled": true, "adaptiveCleanup": true, "cleanupLagThreshold": 1000, "maxConsecutiveCleanupSkips": 3, "lastVerifiedBlockCacheTTL": 900000 } } ``` Here’s how these pieces work together: - **`adaptiveCleanup`**: Enables the lag-aware logic. If left `false` (the default), the node behaves exactly as it always has. - **`cleanupLagThreshold`**: How many blocks behind the node needs to be before it starts skipping cleanup passes. In this example, if the node is more than 1,000 blocks behind head, it postpones pruning. - **`maxConsecutiveCleanupSkips`**: The safety valve. We can't let a node defer cleanup indefinitely while syncing a massive backlog, or local disk usage would balloon. Setting this to `3` means the node will skip at most three consecutive cleanup cycles before forcing a cleanup pass anyway, regardless of lag. - **`lastVerifiedBlockCacheTTL`**: Caches the lookup for `lastVerifiedBlockNumber` in memory for 15 minutes (900,000 ms). That last setting is a quiet efficiency win. Previously, every single cleanup pass did a full database lookup against `witnesses.params` to find the last verified block height. Since round verification only advances every ~40 minutes (~1,200 blocks), re-querying the database every cleanup cycle was pure waste. Because verified block height only moves forward, a cached value is inherently safe: the absolute worst case is that the node retains an extra 15 minutes of old blocks before pruning them. It can never cause the node to delete data too aggressively. ## Live Testing on a 19,000-Block Catch-Up Unit tests are good for checking logic, but I always prefer seeing how these changes behave under actual pressure. I've been running this branch on my live witness setup since October 5th. As luck would have it, my test node ended up falling about **19,000 blocks behind**: giving me a far more realistic stress test than any tidy benchmark I could have staged. Watching `journalctl` during the catch-up confirmed the safety limits were working exactly as designed. The node fell into a predictable rhythm: three skipped cleanup passes followed by one forced cleanup pass, repeating continuously while it processed the backlog. ![screenshot-20261017-092502.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/thecrazygm/23tRtNZZJsvSoXvQgfUVR9YFxNKHz43w9G1WokygUnnPfGsWpSdKyDBTAY9Hu2HsGVrwt.png) Over the course of the run, the logs recorded **90 skipped cleanups and 30 forced cleanups**. The lag steadily dropped from 19,000 blocks down past the 1,000-block threshold, at which point normal periodic cleanup resumed smoothly. The node is now sitting happily locked to the Hive head. ## Designing for Failure: The Fallback Guardrail One detail I was very deliberate about: what happens if the streamer encounters an RPC blip and can't accurately report chain lag? A naive implementation might assume zero lag and clean up constantly, or worse, assume infinite lag and stop cleaning up forever. Instead, if the streamer can't determine current lag, the node logs a clear warning and proceeds with the cleanup pass anyway. It’s always safer to fall back to the established default behavior when an input is uncertain. A kind of defensive edge-case handling that prevents an optimization from turning into a late-night operational headache. ## Status and Verification All of this work is wrapped up in **[PR #141](https://github.com/hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts/pull/141)**, open against the `qa` branch of `hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts`. The PR includes full configuration docs alongside focused database unit tests covering both the cleanup skip decision tree and the cached verified-block lookup (all tests passing cleanly). No complicated magic here: just giving the database a breather when it has higher-priority work on its plate, backed by firm guardrails so the garbage still gets taken out. Give it a look on `qa`, and let me know your thoughts! As always, **Michael Garcia a.k.a. TheCrazyGM**
Source: PR #141: Letting Hive-Engine Lite Nodes Catch Up Before Cleaning House by @thecrazygm

entry.title: Hive Stream Builder: set up a hive-stream app in your browser and download the code

link.title: Hive Stream Builder: set up a hive-stream app in your browser and download the code

entry.content:
If you haven't come across it, [hive-stream](https://github.com/Vheissu/hive-stream) is my Node.js library for building apps on Hive. It's designed to be the ultimate starter library for Hive apps. It streams blocks, runs your contract code when someone calls it with a transfer memo or custom_json, and gives you everything you need to respond, whether that's a payout, a refund or a vote. People use it for dice sites, game tournaments, tipping bots, token exchanges and custody bridges. It comes with 45 ready-made contracts, SQLite, MongoDB and PostgreSQL adapters, a CLI, and since the last update, an offline testing kit. The CLI (`npx hive-stream new`) gets you a starter project, but there's still a fair bit to do after that. You need to work out which built-in contracts you want and what their options are, write a zod schema for each of your actions, add guards to anything that takes money and set up your bot subscriptions. I built Hive Stream Builder to take care of that part. [Hive Stream Builder](https://vheissu.github.io/hive-stream-ui/) is a web app where you configure a hive-stream project and download it as a zip. Everything happens in your browser. There's no backend or account, and it never asks for your keys. You add those to `.env` after downloading. ![hive-stream-builder-project.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/beggars/EqjadgB3D7iQprh3s8Ss2ThCfzQnzpaNSC1bauazVaZZjFetaNrfSkcZj23rEvSL3GW.jpg) The settings are on the left and the generated project is on the right. The code updates as you go, so you can see what each option changes before you download anything. ## Starting point and settings First you pick a starting point. The options are the same templates the CLI has (Minimal, Game, Exchange, Social, Blog, Token & NFT and Assets & Tickets), and the download starts from the exact files the CLI would write. You also choose a database (SQLite, MongoDB or PostgreSQL), set your app's Hive account and decide whether to turn on the HTTP API, which serves contract state, events and a `/health` endpoint on port 5001. The Streamer page covers how your app follows the chain. You can process irreversible blocks only, which is the default and what you want for anything involving money, or follow the head block for lower latency. You can also set how often the block position gets saved, turn on duplicate protection so a replayed block never runs the same action twice, and choose what happens when an action fails: skip it, retry and then stop, or stop straight away. If you tick any hooks like `onError` or `onFork`, you get typed stubs for them in `src/hooks.ts`. Only settings that differ from the defaults are written out, so the config doesn't get bloated. ## Built-in contracts ![hive-stream-builder-catalog.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/beggars/Epi1J4o6NWBR3UhY9pPP3u88k7VschKhmykURjySHPDETRhTzBL3FHTPWR5cYqfJfod.jpg) Every contract that ships with hive-stream is in the catalog, sorted into categories like gambling, games, finance, governance and tokens. The list is pulled from `hive-stream/catalog`, so new contracts show up in the builder as soon as they're added to the library. Once you add a contract you can fill in its options and add guards. Guards let you choose which accounts are allowed or blocked, which assets it accepts, minimum and maximum amounts and a rate limit per account. You can also pause a contract while you do maintenance. ## Custom contracts ![hive-stream-builder-custom-contract.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/beggars/Epi1SFb7qWtTDaMjevU484qe2aGJgzG3d2tvSnNvMnKngZPuBKEWGzCg6vdmudZdjvk.jpg) For your own contracts, you add actions and choose how each one can be called. That can be custom_json, a transfer memo, a schedule, a recurring transfer or one of the escrow operations. You can require the active key for custom_json calls, and you define the payload fields, which become a zod schema so bad payloads get rejected before your code runs. You can also add SQL tables and scheduled jobs. Scheduled jobs run on block time, so they behave the same during a replay as they do live. Each contract is written to `src/contracts/.contract.ts` along with a call spec your frontend can import. It also gets a test that runs every action through `hive-stream/testing`, the offline testing kit I wrote about in my [last Hive Stream post](https://peakd.com/hive-139531/@beggars/hive-stream-grows-up-offline-testing-esm-docs-cli-and-production-plumbing). So the contract you download comes with tests already written. ## Bots ![hive-stream-builder-bots.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/beggars/EqoqQxD96LwHtk4KiFA4iJFUc5FVh9nYqKLDziuE51nJSZraKawsMu2gF4tt4E9uucg.jpg) Bots are rules that react to things happening on chain. Each rule has a trigger, optional conditions and one or more actions. Triggers include transfers, custom_json, posts, comments, votes, Hive Engine actions, escrows and follows. Actions can send HIVE or HBD, refund the sender, send Hive Engine tokens, upvote or write to the log. Each trigger only lets you use the fields it actually has, which means the generated `src/bots.ts` always compiles. ## Call builder ![hive-stream-builder-call-builder.jpg](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/beggars/EnqV25Kfw4zHVSdKySUepJsuiK8VxwUQghs49bqSFdrkAhd8wDcDPZMfqP5zhRQFvWH.jpg) Once your contracts are done you still need to call them from a frontend. In the call builder you pick a contract and an action and fill in the payload. It gives you the transfer memo or custom_json operation, the `hive-stream/client` code, and a Hive Keychain call you can paste into your site. It checks the payload the same way the contract will, and it never broadcasts anything. ## Testing the generated code Generating code is only useful if the code actually works, so the repo has a script for checking it. `npm run verify:generated` generates a project for every template and database combination, a project that uses every feature on each database, and one that registers every built-in contract. It then runs `tsc --noEmit` and the Jest tests on each one against the hive-stream version it pins. It's meant to be run whenever a generator changes or hive-stream gets a new release, which stops the builder falling behind the library. ## Saving and sharing Your project is saved in your browser as you work. You can also copy a share link, which has the whole configuration in the URL, or export it as YAML and import it again later. You can try it at [vheissu.github.io/hive-stream-ui](https://vheissu.github.io/hive-stream-ui/) and the code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/Vheissu/hive-stream-ui). If it ever generates something that doesn't compile, open an issue with your share link and I'll be able to reproduce it. </div>
Source: Hive Stream Builder: set up a hive-stream app in your browser and download the code by @beggars
</div>

entry.title: HAF API stack 1.28.8 release notes: changes since 1.28.6

link.title: HAF API stack 1.28.8 release notes: changes since 1.28.6

entry.content:
<div class="hive-post-embed" data-hive-author="blocktrades" data-hive-permlink="haf-api-stack-1-28-8-release-notes-changes-since-1-28-6"> <div id="content-blocktrades-haf-api-stack-1-28-8-release-notes-changes-since-1-28-6" class="hive-post-embed__content" data-hive-render-target="true">![blocktrades update.png](https://images.hive.blog/DQmSihw8Kz4U7TuCQa98DDdCzqbqPFRumuVWAbareiYZW1Z/blocktrades%20update.png)
This report is written for several kinds of readers: people who use Hive apps and wallets, developers building on Hive, and API node operators. Most readers will only need some of it, so feel free to skip the sections that don't apply to you.
There were too many changes this time, so the initial version was written by scanning the commit history using AI, then reviewed and modified by the devs who worked on the changes. It includes most changes to hived, HAF, the HAF apps and the haf\_api\_node deployment stack between the 1.28.6 release (2026-05-04) and the 1.28.8 release (tagged yesterday, deployed today). hive and haf also had a small 1.28.7 hotfix tag (2026-07-10); its changes are included here and marked [1.28.7].
## Scope
| Repo | Role | Commits 1.28.6..1.28.8 | | --- | --- | --- | | hive | hived blockchain node, cli\_wallet | 224 | | haf | sql\_serializer plugin, hive\_fork\_manager extension, HAF image | 65 | | hivemind | Social / condenser API app | 37 | | HAfAH | Account history API app | 14 | | balance\_tracker | Balances, vesting, transfer stats app | 79 | | reputation\_tracker | Reputation app | 27 | | haf\_block\_explorer | Block explorer backend app | 82 | | nft\_tracker | NFT app | 18 | | hivesense | Semantic search (embeddings) app | 38 | | haf\_api\_node | Docker Compose stack for API nodes | 67 |
## Read first: what an upgrade from 1.28.6 involves
- **Replay:** Full replay required, or download a full 1.28.8 snapshot. hived's in-memory state layout changed, and HAF's schema changed (new `rc_cost` column, new app-registry tables). HAF's in-place extension update refuses to run on the schema-hash mismatch. Since HAF is replayed, every HAF app resyncs from scratch too. - **PostgreSQL:** HAF now runs on PostgreSQL 18. The replay builds the new database on 18. - **Ubuntu 26.04:** The hived and HAF Docker images moved from Ubuntu 24.04 to Ubuntu 26.04 (Boost 1.90, Python 3.14). The reference build environment is now Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15, Boost 1.90 and CMake 4, and hived requires C++20. The other HAF app images don't change OS. - **API:** `get_dynamic_global_properties` no longer returns `total_reward_fund_hive` or `total_reward_shares2`. balance\_tracker `/transfer-statistics` amounts are now `{nai, amount, precision}` objects, and stats `date` now labels the period start. - **Stack:** haf\_api\_node: create `${HAF_LOG_DIRECTORY}/apps` before `up`, and note that p2p port 2001 is now published by default. - No mainnet consensus changes. Mainnet still has 28 hardforks; HF29 work exists only on testnet and mirrornet.
## 1. Features that affect users
Changes visible to people using Hive frontends, wallets and the public APIs.
#### Network reliability
- Nodes are much more resilient to the kind of p2p disruption seen on 2026-07-09. They stop mass-disconnecting peers over slightly stale blocks, recover automatically when stuck behind, and keep dialing peers when DNS or routing is limited. Details are under bug fixes. ([b31dd12269](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/b31dd12269) [16a419df6a](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/16a419df6a) [9040b581c8](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/9040b581c8) [73b937e98f](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/73b937e98f)) - IPv6 p2p connections now work end to end, and nodes prefer IPv6 peers when both are available. ([18e482508b](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/18e482508b) [9112cde237](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/9112cde237))
#### Wallet
- cli\_wallet refuses to save if another process changed the wallet file since it was loaded, and writes through a temp file plus atomic rename, so a second wallet instance can no longer silently overwrite keys. ([bfad335466](https://gitlab.syncad.com/hive/hive/-/commit/bfad335466))
#### Social and rewards (hivemind)

entry.title: hivetop :: a cli hive monitor
entry.content:
# hivetop
`hivetop` is an htop-like terminal monitor for the Hive blockchain. It follows blocks through Hive JSON-RPC, aggregates recent block/transaction/operation rates, and renders a live terminal dashboard. ## Installation Requires **Node 24 or newer**. With nvm, run `nvm install 24`. Install the command from [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/hivetop): ```bash npm install --global hivetop hivetop ``` Or run it without a global install: ```bash npx hivetop ``` ## Usage Run `hivetop --help` for command-line options. Run `hivetop` from any directory. Examples: ```bash hivetop --view round hivetop --view sizes hivetop --view txstatus --compact --ascii hivetop --node https://api.hive.blog hivetop --start 98765432 hivetop --window 120 --poll-ms 1000 hivetop --follow --node https://api.hive.blog --limit 42 NO_COLOR=1 hivetop ``` The four views are blocks, the witness schedule (`round`), transaction status (`txstatus`, the defrag view), and block-size history (`sizes`). `--view` chooses the starting view. ![Screenshot 2026-10-06 at 2.30.41 PM.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/inertia/23uQNa9RmbnK7ENio9KMHMX4yyPPukinboMpMjvYeHERrD3daXx9ayoxjBADk7DAfNFJP.png) ![Screenshot 2026-10-06 at 2.30.58 PM.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/inertia/23uEz3vXzyuMiVpjq84FmPNWFSfNvrPBEjJt1zdq2zJFVkhECGXcPv76vcrG14ba2aceL.png) ![Screenshot 2026-10-06 at 2.31.05 PM.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/inertia/23y8miukvPqM3Axyvo2dm6JyTtwuygns14q1NMCvXVqMTmxfB2sQeEs26RN6NhMWS8gXb.png) ![Screenshot 2026-10-06 at 2.32.04 PM.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/inertia/23vsDhWHVC3RCsi6tBXohM92UoQR8Va3nhmx5NfzwaibStsTpSmHPu7CE6HB6Mjtvv4m7.png) The witness view previews the announced next round and marks the current round with `>`, its block range, and progress. Its live position keeps the latest produced block visible alongside predictions. The `sizes` view plots uncompressed serialized block bytes over the rolling `--window` (120 seconds by default), oldest on the left and newest on the right. It shows the latest measured size, mean, minimum, and peak. The vertical scale adapts to the peak in the window; axes use KiB (1024 bytes) and UTC time. Blocks sharing a chart column use their peak size. Empty or unmeasured slots stay blank. `--ascii` uses `#` for the filled chart. Light bar faces and darker right edges give each block a shadow, including adjacent blocks of equal size. `--no-color` keeps the chart monochrome. Size measurements run in the background only while this view is visible. Each block needs an extra block fetch and one `get_transaction_hex` call; operations are serialized together, with the original transaction headers, signatures, signed block header, and transaction count included in the total. Backfilling is limited to at most one measurement per second. The measured/total block count shows progress while recent history fills in. Failures appear in the view and event history, retry after 30 seconds, and leave block tracking running. Measured sizes remain available in block details. `--compact` hides the sidebar and reduces the number of columns. Narrow terminals adapt automatically. `--ascii` replaces graphical status cells with distinct letters. `--no-color` or a nonempty `NO_COLOR` disables colors and also uses status letters, so the transaction map remains readable. By default, `hivetop` asks [PeakD Beacon](https://beacon.peakd.com/api/nodes) for available Hive API nodes. It follows `api.hive.blog` while its Beacon score is at least `90`; below that threshold, it switches to the highest-scored node that advertises `get_rc_stats`. During runtime it uses the same Beacon-ordered node list for basic failover when RPC calls fail. Pass `--node` to pin a specific endpoint and disable Beacon failover. Each RPC request, including its response body, has a 10-second deadline; override it with `--rpc-timeout-ms MS`. The header shows the age of the latest received block and the most recent RPC response time. `STALE` means the node's head or the last data update is over 15 seconds old; `RECONNECTING` means the block RPC failed and is being retried. Cached rates describe the last received block window. While catching up, the block age refers to the followed block. RC stats, hardfork info, and witness ranks refresh independently of block tracking. Failed metadata requests retain last-known values, display an unavailable/stale notice, and retry after 30 seconds. The schedule is fetched with the block context; if unavailable, blocks still advance and the last-known schedule remains subject to its normal prediction expiry. The dashboard uses the terminal's alternate screen and restores the cursor and normal input mode when you quit, press Ctrl-C, or send SIGTERM. Redirected output requires `--follow`. Use `--follow` for investigation: it prints one JSON diagnostic record per block instead of opening the terminal UI. Pair it with `--limit NUM` to stop after a bounded number of produced block records. JSON diagnostics use the same accepted schedule, absolute slot, and shuffle boundary logic as the display. `future_block` and `future_scheduled` identify the first predicted block in the next round. `reported_schedule_sig` and `reported_next_shuffle_block_num` preserve what the node reported when it differs from the accepted schedule. `--limit` counts produced blocks and terminal gaps; an unavailable block is skipped after three retries in diagnostic mode. Keyboard controls: - `q` or `Ctrl-C`: quit - `p`: pause/resume rendering and block fetching - `r`: reset the follower to the current head block - `v`: cycle blocks, witness round, transaction status, and block sizes - Arrow keys / `j` / `k`: select a row (`*` marks the selection) - PageUp / PageDown: move by a page; Home / `g`: return to live rows - Enter: inspect the selected produced block, its transactions, and operation counts - `/`: filter by witness name; Enter applies the filter - `?`: help and legends - `e`: scrollable event history, newest first - Esc: close help/details/history, cancel input, or clear the witness filter Block details use data already received from the node. Future blocks become inspectable after production. The local event history retains the latest 100 entries for this session: missed blocks, node changes, connection states, RPC errors, metadata failures, and schedule discrepancies. It is not written to disk. ASCII transaction legend: `*` checking, `I` irreversible, `R` reversible, `.` pending, `?` unknown, `M` mempool, `E` expired, `T` old, `!` block mismatch. Stretched cells share one transaction's status. In the witness view, `√` (ASCII `+`) means the expected witness produced, `x` means a miss backed by chain evidence, and `?` means the schedule is unverified. The VERSION cell is highlighted yellow when it differs from the majority witness version. The FEED cell is highlighted yellow after 6 hours and red at 24 hours, so the reason for a witness's different appearance is visible. ## Troubleshooting ### The `hivetop` command is not found With nvm, global commands belong to the selected Node installation. Run `nvm use 24`, then `npm install --global hivetop`. For a local checkout, run `npm link` from the repository instead. ### Colors or status cells look wrong Try `hivetop --ascii --no-color`. For cramped layouts, add `--compact`. When reporting display problems, include your terminal app, font, and a screenshot, since rendering can differ between terminals. ### The dashboard shows `STALE` or `RECONNECTING` Press `e` to inspect recent RPC errors and node changes. Automatic node selection retries requests and fails over when needed; an explicit `--node` pins the endpoint. Restart without `--node` to restore automatic selection. For a short diagnostic capture: ```bash hivetop --follow --limit 5 ``` ## Development The runtime is dependency-free and checked into `dist/` so it can run without installing packages. TypeScript source lives in `src/`; after installing dependencies, `npm run build` regenerates `dist/`. To install the command from this checkout: ```bash nvm use npm ci npm link ``` The command links to this checkout, so pulling updates also updates the command. With nvm, the link belongs to the selected Node installation; use `nvm use 24` in new shells if needed. `npm start` also runs the app directly from the checkout. ```bash npm test npm run build ``` GitHub Actions runs the tests on Node 24 and verifies that rebuilding does not change the checked-in `dist/` files. Run `npm ci` after cloning to install the development tools. Runtime dependencies are provided by Node itself. ## Contributing Bug reports, feature requests, and pull requests are welcome on [GitHub](https://github.com/inertia186/hivetop). When [opening an issue](https://github.com/inertia186/hivetop/issues), include the command you ran, your Node version (`node --version`), and steps to reproduce the problem. Before submitting a pull request, run `npm test`. It rebuilds `dist/` before running the tests; include any regenerated runtime files with source changes. ## Publishing From this repository with Node 24 or newer: ```bash npm ci npm login npm publish --access public ``` Publishing builds the runtime and runs the tests first. The package includes only `dist/`, `package.json`, this README, the logo, and the license. Use `npm pack --dry-run` to review the file list before publishing. ## Get in touch! If you're using hivetop, I'd love to hear from you. Drop me a line and tell me what you think! I'm [@inertia](https://hive.blog/@inertia) on Hive. ## License I don't believe in intellectual "property". If you do, consider hivetop as licensed under [Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal](LICENSE).

entry.title: Upgrading MongoDB 8 to 9: Why Systemd Refused to Start and How to Bridge the FCV Gap

link.title: Upgrading MongoDB 8 to 9: Why Systemd Refused to Start and How to Bridge the FCV Gap

entry.content:
Hey everyone, If you run a Hive-Engine node (or manage a self-hosted MongoDB instance on Linux), you might run into a nasty surprise after bumping your apt repositories for MongoDB 9.0. You configure the official repository, run `sudo apt update && sudo apt dist-upgrade`, let the package manager do its thing, and wait for `mongod` to spin back up. Except it doesn't. `systemctl status mongod` shows the service failed immediately on boot with exit code `62`, leaving you staring at an offline database and wondering whether your node's 400+ GB dataset just got toasted. The good news: your data is completely fine. The catch: you've stepped right into MongoDB's rapid release compatibility trap. Here is what went wrong, why MongoDB 9.0 flat-out refused to boot, and the step-by-step process to safely bridge the gap (including the replica set details that Hive-Engine strictly enforces) so you can get your node back online with zero data loss. --- ## The Symptoms: Exit Code 62 on Startup Immediately after upgrading packages from MongoDB 8.2 to 9.0, `systemctl status mongod` reported: ```text × mongod.service - MongoDB Database Server Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/mongod.service; enabled; preset: enabled) Active: failed (Result: exit-code) Process: 3053614 ExecStart=/usr/bin/mongod --config /etc/mongod.conf (code=exited, status=62) Main PID: 3053614 (code=exited, status=62) ``` Exit code `62` in MongoDB means server initialization failed during startup checks before opening network listeners. To see the real reason, checking `/var/log/mongodb/mongod.log` (or `journalctl -u mongod`) revealed this fatal log entry: ```json { "s": "F", "c": "CONTROL", "id": 20573, "ctx": "initandlisten", "msg": "Wrong mongod version", "attr": { "error": "UPGRADE PROBLEM: Found an invalid featureCompatibilityVersion document (ERROR: Location4926900: Invalid featureCompatibilityVersion document in admin.system.version: { _id: \"featureCompatibilityVersion\", version: \"8.2\" }. See https://docs.mongodb.com/master/release-notes/8.0-compatibility/#feature-compatibility. :: caused by :: Invalid feature compatibility version value '8.2'. Expected one of the following versions: '9.0', '8.3', '8.0'.)" } } ``` Notice the crucial detail: > **`Invalid feature compatibility version value '8.2'. Expected one of the following versions: '9.0', '8.3', '8.0'.`** Immediately after emitting this error, `mongod` initiated an orderly rollback checkpoint and shut itself down cleanly without touching or modifying any user collections. --- ## Why Did This Happen? The Rapid Release Trap MongoDB follows two release tracks: 1. **Major / LTS Releases:** (e.g., 7.0, 8.0, 9.0) 2. **Rapid Releases:** quarterly minor feature releases between major versions (e.g., 8.1, 8.2, 8.3) Every MongoDB database contains an internal setting called `featureCompatibilityVersion` (FCV) stored in the `admin.system.version` collection. FCV controls which on-disk features, file structures, and internal behaviors the engine is permitted to use. MongoDB enforces strict rules when upgrading: - You cannot skip versions. - A major release binary only knows how to handle datasets from the **previous LTS release** (e.g., FCV `8.0`) or the **final rapid release** immediately preceding the new major version (e.g., FCV `8.3`). Because my machine was previously tracking the rapid release channel on **MongoDB 8.2** (`8.2.12`), its internal FCV was set to `"8.2"`. When the MongoDB 9.0 binary checked the metadata at startup, it saw an FCV of `"8.2"`. But 9.0 only knows about `'8.0'`, `'8.3'`, and `'9.0'`. It does not support jumping directly from 8.2 to 9.0. Furthermore, you cannot simply tell 8.2 to downgrade its FCV to 8.0. MongoDB only allows setting FCV to its current minor version or the immediately prior one (8.2 or 8.1). The only supported bridge to 9.0 is **MongoDB 8.3**. --- ## The Hive-Engine Factor: Replica Sets Are Mandatory There is another crucial detail every node operator must know: **Hive-Engine strictly forces MongoDB to run as a replica set** (typically `replSetName: "rs0"` in `/etc/mongod.conf`), even when running on a single local server. Hive-Engine relies heavily on multi-document ACID transactions and change stream / oplog tailing to process smart contracts deterministically. A standalone MongoDB instance simply will not run Hive-Engine. This requirement introduces three essential rules during this upgrade process: 1. **Startup is not instantaneous:** Every time `mongod` starts, it must initialize its replication coordinator, replay the oplog, and run an election to become `PRIMARY`. 2. **FCV commands require PRIMARY state:** You cannot execute `db.adminCommand({ setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: ... })` while the node is in `STARTUP`, `STARTUP2`, or `SECONDARY`. Running it too quickly after starting systemd will fail with an error like `node is not primary` or `not master and slaveOk=false`. 3. **Always verify replication health:** Before shutting down 8.3 (and after bringing up 9.0), you must check `rs.status()` to ensure the replica set is fully caught up and healthy. --- ## The Solution: The 8.3 Stepping Stone The fix is a sequential upgrade: 1. Temporarily install **MongoDB 8.3**. 2. Boot the 8.3 service (which understands FCV `8.2`). 3. Raise `featureCompatibilityVersion` to `"8.3"`. 4. Shut down 8.3. 5. Upgrade to **MongoDB 9.0**. 6. Boot 9.0 (which accepts FCV `"8.3"`). 7. Finalize `featureCompatibilityVersion` to `"9.0"`. Here is the exact playbook to execute this safely on Debian/Ubuntu systems. --- ### Step 1: Temporarily Add the MongoDB 8.3 Repository Create a temporary APT sources file for MongoDB 8.3. MongoDB 8.3 uses the 8.0 signing key: ```bash sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mongodb-org-8.3.sources << 'EOF' Types: deb URIs: https://repo.mongodb.org/apt/debian/ Suites: bookworm/mongodb-org/8.3 Components: main Architectures: amd64 Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/mongodb-server-8.0.gpg EOF ``` > (Note: Adjust the suite name if using Ubuntu or another Debian distribution codename.) Update your package index: ```bash sudo apt update ``` --- ### Step 2: Downgrade Packages to MongoDB 8.3 Before downgrading, back up your MongoDB configuration just in case: ```bash sudo cp -p /etc/mongod.conf /etc/mongod.conf.bak ``` Now install the MongoDB 8.3 packages (specifying version `8.3.11` or the latest available 8.3 build) and pass `--allow-downgrades`: ```bash sudo apt install -y --allow-downgrades -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" \ mongodb-org=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-server=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-database=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-database-tools-extra=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-mongos=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-shell=8.3.11 \ mongodb-org-tools=8.3.11 ``` Confirm that the binary is now on 8.3: ```bash mongod --version ``` You should see: ```text db version v8.3.11 ``` --- ### Step 3: Start MongoDB 8.3 and Advance FCV to 8.3 Start the systemd service: ```bash sudo systemctl start mongod sudo systemctl status mongod ``` Because MongoDB 8.3 supports datasets with FCV `8.2`, it will start up cleanly. #### Wait for Replica Set Election (Mandatory for Hive-Engine) Because Hive-Engine enforces running as a replica set, give `mongod` a few seconds after startup to initialize the replication coordinator and elect itself `PRIMARY`. If you attempt to update the feature compatibility version while the node is still in `STARTUP2` or `SECONDARY`, the command will be rejected. Confirm that your node has finished election and is `PRIMARY`: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "rs.status().members[0].stateStr" ``` You should see: ```text PRIMARY ``` Once confirmed `PRIMARY`, inspect the current FCV: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 })" ``` Output: ```json { "featureCompatibilityVersion": { "version": "8.2" }, "ok": 1 } ``` Now upgrade the feature compatibility version to 8.3: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: '8.3', confirm: true })" ``` Verify that the transition succeeded: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 })" ``` It should now display: ```json { "featureCompatibilityVersion": { "version": "8.3" }, "ok": 1 } ``` Confirm replica set health and write availability one more time before stopping the daemon: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "rs.status().ok" ``` --- ### Step 4: Stop 8.3 and Clean Up the Temporary Repo Stop the service cleanly: ```bash sudo systemctl stop mongod ``` Remove the temporary 8.3 repository so APT doesn't get confused: ```bash sudo rm -f /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mongodb-org-8.3.sources sudo apt update ``` --- ### Step 5: Upgrade Back to MongoDB 9.0 Ensure your 9.0 repository file (e.g. `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/mongodb-org-9.0.sources`) is active: ```bash cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mongodb-org-9.0.sources ``` ```text Types: deb URIs: https://repo.mongodb.org/apt/debian/ Suites: trixie/mongodb-org/9.0 Components: main Architectures: amd64 Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/mongodb-server-9.gpg ``` Run the upgrade back to MongoDB 9.0: ```bash sudo apt upgrade -y -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" \ mongodb-org \ mongodb-org-server \ mongodb-org-database \ mongodb-org-database-tools-extra \ mongodb-org-mongos \ mongodb-org-shell \ mongodb-org-tools ``` Verify the binary is back on version 9.0: ```bash mongod --version ``` ![screenshot-20261005-113234.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/thecrazygm/23t72p136b8msyb9C4vyKZMMefbe3xRux7CSZdSCi7DviGGu7PjuBpnUMH2FuKCjbVQir.png) ```text db version v9.0.2 ``` --- ### Step 6: Start MongoDB 9.0 and Finalize FCV to 9.0 Start `mongod.service`: ```bash sudo systemctl start mongod sudo systemctl status mongod ``` Check the status: the service should now report `active (running)`. #### Confirm Replica Set Primary State Once again, give the daemon a moment to finish its replica set election. Before attempting to update the FCV to 9.0, make sure the node is in `PRIMARY` state: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "rs.status().members[0].stateStr" ``` Output: ```text PRIMARY ``` Next, connect with `mongosh` and inspect the current FCV: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 })" ``` It will show that 9.0 is currently running in backward-compatibility mode with FCV `8.3`. Finally, lock in the 9.0 features by advancing the compatibility version: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ setFeatureCompatibilityVersion: '9.0', confirm: true })" ``` Verify the final status: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, featureCompatibilityVersion: 1 })" ``` Output: ```json { "featureCompatibilityVersion": { "version": "9.0" }, "ok": 1 } ``` Lastly, verify that your replica set and Hive-Engine databases (`hsc`, `hsc_history`, etc.) are healthy and reporting correctly: ```bash mongosh --quiet --eval "rs.status().ok" mongosh --quiet --eval "db.adminCommand({ listDatabases: 1 })" ``` Everything is now fully migrated, running MongoDB 9.0 natively, and all your databases and collections remain intact. --- ## Summary of Key Takeaways 1. **Never skip MongoDB intermediate rapid releases when targeting a new LTS major.** MongoDB 9.0 only supports incoming datasets with FCV `8.0` (from the prior LTS) or `8.3` (from the final rapid release). 2. **Exit Code 62 with `Wrong mongod version` is non-destructive.** MongoDB refuses to touch database files when an FCV mismatch is encountered. Do not panic and do not run `mongod --repair` blindly. 3. **Hive-Engine forces replica sets:** Because Hive-Engine requires a replica set for multi-document transactions and oplog processing, MongoDB nodes must complete election and achieve `PRIMARY` status on every restart before FCV commands can be executed. Running FCV updates during `STARTUP2` will fail. 4. **The bridge technique works smoothly with APT:** By temporarily pulling in the missing intermediate release (8.3), you can boot the daemon, advance the internal FCV document, and then proceed with the target major release upgrade cleanly. As always, **Michael Garcia** a.k.a. **TheCrazyGM**
Source: Upgrading MongoDB 8 to 9: Why Systemd Refused to Start and How to Bridge the FCV Gap by @thecrazygm

entry.title: Tin Toy - Hive 1.29.0 on a Local Testnet

link.title: Tin Toy - Hive 1.29.0 on a Local Testnet

entry.content:
Tin Toy has a new core release for Hive 1.29.0. The idea is still the same: a small local testnet for working on Hive applications without broadcasting your experiments to mainnet. There are a couple of changes worth calling out before you copy a command from an older tintoy post. #### The core image The current image starts hived, applies the sample snapshot through Tinman, and sets up 21 deterministic witnesses. RPC is now on port 8092; p2p is on 2001. The old Jussi, nginx, Postgres, Hivemind, condenser, and Tinman-server files are still in the gist as reference material, but those services aren't started or exposed by this image. If your app depends on Hivemind's content APIs, that part of the old stack isn't included in the current core release. #### Try it out With Docker running Linux containers, the README's quick start is: ```bash docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --name tintoy \ -p 8092:8092 \ -p 2001:2001 \ inertia/tintoy:1.29.0 ``` Python, Tinman, and Hive are included. The command assumes a Bash-compatible shell, so use WSL or Git Bash on Windows. ARM hosts, including Apple Silicon, need AMD64 emulation. This is a disposable testnet with deterministic keys. Keep it off untrusted networks. For a Docker daemon on your own machine, use `-p 127.0.0.1:8092:8092` and `-p 127.0.0.1:2001:2001` to bind the published ports to localhost. Allow several minutes for bootstrap. Look for this message: ``` tintoy: snapshot applied and seed node is producing ``` Then, from another terminal, check the RPC endpoint. This command uses curl and jq on your host: ```bash curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8092 \ --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"database_api.get_dynamic_global_properties","params":{},"id":1}' \ | jq ``` Run it twice, a few seconds apart. `head_block_number` should increase. #### Which tag? - `1.29.0`: the current Hive 1.29.0 core testnet - `latest`: currently the same 1.29.0 release - `1.28.7`: the Hive 1.28.7 release built for testnet - `core-2026.10.03`: the original dated core release, also using Hive 1.29.0 - `legacy-2021`: the previous May 2021 image, with its historical services and ports One detail about `1.28.7`: its testnet binary reports blockchain version `1.28.6`. That's how the upstream release is defined. The image includes the release's peer-handling fixes; the image tag and the reported blockchain version describe different things. Also, `latest` now points to the core release. An old port-8090 command won't give you the same stack it did in 2021. #### Building from source The current Dockerfile uses pinned Tinman and Hive images. From a checkout of [the gist](https://gist.github.com/inertia186/b88e7bfff8862858e54c59392e2bce20), build with: ```bash docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t tintoy:local . ``` The [README](https://gist.github.com/inertia186/b88e7bfff8862858e54c59392e2bce20#file-readme-md) has the build arguments for trying other image combinations. Use immutable image digests when you need a reproducible result. The documented checks cover the 2,000-account sample, registration and scheduling of all 21 replacement witnesses, and advancing blocks. The current Tinman pin has passed fresh Docker Desktop AMD64-emulation bootstraps with both Hive 1.29.0 and 1.28.7. If you need a little chain to develop against, that's the starting point: bring it up, check that blocks are moving, and point your app at the local RPC endpoint. [Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/inertia/tintoy) · [Source and README](https://gist.github.com/inertia186/b88e7bfff8862858e54c59392e2bce20)
